questions.prompt: Why do products use RAG instead of pasting all company documents into every prompt?

options.text: Documents would fill (or overflow) the context window and cost far more per call — retrieval sends only the relevant passages
Models refuse to read more than one document
It's illegal to send documents to an API
RAG retrains the model on the documents each night

questions.explanation: Context is a scarce, priced resource. Like a library index, RAG fetches only the few passages that matter and puts just those in the prompt. It never retrains the model — that would be fine-tuning, next lesson.

options.text: A compressed zip file of a document
A list of numbers representing a text's meaning, so similar meanings end up numerically close together
A keyword list extracted from a document
A smaller copy of the language model

questions.explanation: Embeddings are coordinates for meaning. 'Reset my password' and 'password recovery steps' share almost no words but land near each other — which is why embedding search beats keyword search for questions.

questions.prompt: At question time, what does a RAG system do FIRST with the user's question?

options.text: Sends it straight to the LLM for an answer
Embeds the question and searches the index for the nearest document chunks
Asks the user to pick which document to search
Fine-tunes the model on the question

questions.explanation: Question → embedding → nearest-neighbor search → paste the retrieved chunks plus the question into the prompt → model answers grounded in those chunks.

questions.prompt: Which are real ways a RAG system can still give a wrong answer? (select all that apply)

options.text: The retriever fetched the wrong passages, so the model never saw the answer
The index is stale — the documents changed after they were embedded
Retrieval returned junk and the model guessed from its training instead
RAG systems cannot give wrong answers

questions.explanation: RAG grounds answers but every stage can fail: bad retrieval, stale index, or the model improvising when the retrieved text doesn't contain the answer. Trust but verify — especially citations.
